content_voiceover: This is the treatment algorithm for idiopathic multicentric Castleman disease, and it's risk-stratified by five severity criteria: ECOG performance status two or worse, renal failure with GFR under thirty, anemia with hemoglobin under eight, widespread serous effusions, and pulmonary involvement. Zero out of five criteria means asymptomatic disease, and the answer is simply observation, no treatment, just regular monitoring for progression. One out of five criteria is non-severe disease, and first-line therapy is siltuximab, an anti-IL-6 monoclonal antibody, with or without oral steroids, or alternatively thalidomide plus rituximab with or without steroids. If that gives an adequate response, you move to maintenance siltuximab or thalidomide; if inadequate, escalate to combination chemotherapy. Two or more out of five criteria defines severe disease, including TAFRO syndrome, and that demands anti-IL-6 therapy plus high-dose parenteral steroids, or combination chemotherapy like R-CHOP or R-CVP. A good response there gets maintenance siltuximab, while an inadequate response should prompt referral to clinical trials, since options run out fast at that severity tier. The key teaching point is that siltuximab, targeting IL-6, is the backbone first-line agent across the non-severe and severe pathways, reflecting IL-6's central role in iMCD pathophysiology.
keypoints: 5 severity criteria: ECOG 2 or worse, renal failure (GFR under 30), anemia (Hb under 8), serous effusions, pulmonary involvement
1/5 criteria = non-severe, siltuximab with or without steroids, or thalidomide plus rituximab with or without steroids
2 or more/5 criteria = severe (including TAFRO), anti-IL-6 plus high-dose steroids or combination chemo (R-CHOP/R-CVP)
Siltuximab (anti-IL-6) is the backbone agent, reflecting IL-6-driven pathophysiology
